whyThisIdea: Este prima idee nefolosită din backlog (#9) și nu se suprapune cu articolele publicate. Se leagă de articolul despre citit (aceleași 122 de ore pe an, 20 de minute pe zi) și de faptul că scrii blogul și te uiți la alții înainte să scrii.

entry.title: Comparison is a tax on attention.
entry.titleHtml: Comparison is a tax on attention.
entry.dek: Follow 300 people who post their best moment once a week and you see about 43 highlights a day. You are comparing your average with their best.
body: “You only ever see their final version. You live inside your first draft.”

Have you ever asked yourself what you were actually doing in the last ten minutes before you started something important? Today is Monday, the 9th of November, and this morning I opened the document for this article, wrote one sentence, and then opened another tab “just to see” how other people write about the same thing. Twenty minutes later I had read three of their posts, looked at how many people follow them, and my own page still had one sentence on it. So the question is: why does looking at somebody else’s work cost so much of the time I wanted for mine? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is comparison, and I met it in the most obvious place - this blog. Before I started it, comparing was easy, because I had nothing to compare. Now I have a page with my name on it, and every other page on the internet looks like a mirror. Someone writes better, someone has more readers, someone posts every day and makes it look like it costs nothing. None of them did anything to me. And still, I noticed that I come back from their pages a little bit smaller and a lot less ready to write.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “Comparison” and “tax”. Comparison is not a modern invention and it is not a weakness. In 1954 the psychologist Leon Festinger published a paper called “A Theory of Social Comparison Processes”, and his idea was simple: people have a drive to evaluate their own opinions and abilities, and when there is no objective measure, they use other people as the measure. There is no ruler for “is my writing good”, so I look at other writers. That part is normal. The “tax” part is what I added, because a tax is something you pay whether you agree with it or not, and it is taken before you even see the money. Comparison is taken from your attention before you ever get to use it.

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic on what we are comparing ourselves with, because I think this is where the whole problem is. This is an example I built, not a measurement. Say you follow 300 accounts and each of them posts their best moment once a week - the trip, the result, the finished project.
300 ÷ 7 = about 43 highlights a day
300 × 52 = 15.600 highlights a year
Against that, you have 365 days of your own, and you see all of them - the boring ones, the tired ones, the ones where you wrote one sentence. So for every ordinary day of yours, you see about 43 of the best days of other people. You are not comparing your life with their life, you are comparing your average with their best. No wonder the result always looks bad.

And the cost is not only in how you feel, it is also in minutes. Say you spend 20 minutes a day on other people’s highlights while your own work waits.
20 minutes × 365 days = 7.300 minutes
7.300 ÷ 60 = about 122 hours a year
If that number sounds familiar, it is because I counted the same 122 hours a few days ago, in the article about reading, for 20 minutes a day with a book. Same minutes, same year. One version ends with books read, the other ends with a long list of people who are doing better than you.

Now let’s look at a real study, because so far all the numbers were mine. In 2013, Ethan Kross and his colleagues at the University of Michigan published a study in PLOS ONE with a title that does not try to be nice: “Facebook use predicts declines in subjective well-being in young adults”. They followed 82 young adults and sent them a text message five times a day for 14 days, asking how they felt and how much they had used Facebook since the last message. The more people used Facebook, the worse they felt the next time they were asked, and the more they used it over the two weeks, the more their life satisfaction went down. And the detail I find the most interesting: talking with people directly, face to face or on the phone, did not have that effect. It was not people that made them feel worse, it was the feed.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Festinger did not say comparison is bad, he said it is how we find out where we are. And I would be lying if I said comparison never helped me. I started this blog partly because I read other people’s writing and thought “I want to do that”. So the problem is not looking at other people. The problem is what you look at and when. Looking at how someone built their article, slowly, line by line, teaches me something. Looking at their number of followers while my own draft is open teaches me nothing, it only takes. And there is one comparison that is always fair, because I see every day of both sides: me against the version of me from September, when the first review went up.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. For the rest of the week, the rule is simple: no other blogs, no feeds, nothing of anybody else until today’s writing is done. After that, read anything you want. And at the end of the week I will put my first article next to my last one and compare only those two. If there is a difference, that is the only comparison I want to pay for.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the idea is right, but I have to be fair about the evidence. The Kross study had only 82 people, followed for two weeks, and it was about Facebook in 2013, which is not the same thing as the apps we use today. It shows that using it and feeling worse go together over time, it does not prove one causes the other. My 43 highlights a day is an example I made up to make a point, not a fact about anybody’s phone. And I do not want to pretend comparison is the enemy, because without it I would not even know what good writing looks like. What I take from it is smaller: compare yourself with people when you want to learn something, and with yourself when you want to know how you are doing.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“You only ever see their final version. You live inside your first draft.”
